I.         INTRODUCTION

           This proceeding involves the Joint Application of Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC

and LCRA Transmission Service Corporation to amend their Certificates of Convenience and

Necessity for the Bell County East Switch to Big Hill Substation 765-kV Transmission Line

Project, a proposed high-voltage transmission line spanning approximately 223 miles across

fifteen Texas counties. 1         In an alternative finding, the ALJs determined that, should the

Commission approve the Application, Route 894 best meets the routing criteria set forth under

PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(A)-(D) and PUC Substantive Rule 25.101(b)(3)(B). 2 These Exceptions

focus on that “best meets” recommendation.

           The Brady Creek Intervenors except, to the extent the Commission approves the

Application, to the ALJs’ recommendation of Route 894, and to the due process deficiencies

addressed in Section VI below that prevented full development of the routing record. As set forth

herein, the record establishes that Route 392, not Route 894, best satisfies the routing criteria the

Commission must apply. Alternatively, Route 410 preserves many of the advantages of Route 392

       D. Hearing on the Merits

       The Hearing on the Merits (“HOM”) was conducted over five days, June 8 through June

12, 2026, and required the parties to litigate 823 filed witness testimonies and 1,398 admitted

exhibits. Time for cross-examination in this proceeding was compressed past the point of

impinging on parties’ due process rights. Each attorney was allowed 13 minutes for cross

examination of the companies’ panel of eight witnesses. The time limit was enforced at 13 minutes

per law firm, effectively, whether that attorney or firm represented one party miles away from any

route of interest, multiple parties situated on one segment, or, as did the undersigned, two groups

of landowners, over 130 miles distant from one another, each bisected by the Applicants’ proposed

“best meets” route, and potentially impacted by other proposed links. Similarly, each attorney was

allowed only seven minutes to cross examine PUC Staff witness John Poole, and only three

minutes each for cross examination of any other intervenor witness.

            Put another way, the ALJs allotted a single block of cross-examination time for each

witness or panel, to be shared by all cross-examining parties represented by common counsel,

without regard to whether those parties were separately constituted intervenor groups with distinct

properties, witnesses, and routes at issue.

           Because the Brady Creek Intervenors’ counsel also represented the Solana Intervenors, an

unrelated intervenor with property situated approximately 130 miles away in the Study Area, the

Brady Creek Intervenors and the Solana Intervenors jointly moved on June 7, 2026, to allocate

each group its own block of cross-examination time for the six witnesses or panels independently

designated for cross-examination by both groups, including the Applicants’ panel. 3

           The ALJs denied that motion, denied counsel’s renewed request at the close of the

Applicants’ panel’s direct examination, and denied reconsideration. 4 As a result, the Brady Creek

Intervenors were denied a fair opportunity to cross-examine the Applicants’ panel, Commission

Staff, and intervenor witnesses on subjects material to the routing determination. For example,

Route 894, the “best meets” route in this case, utilizes Link K13 and K51. Those two links are the

closest in the entire Study Area to Links K2, K3, and J5, which appeared on the routing maps

presented at the public meeting and open house stage of this proceeding but were subsequently

dropped from the filed Application.

           The Applicants’ Environmental Assessment stated that Link K2, K3 and J5 were removed

due to “significant environmental impacts” and specially referenced proximity to the San Saba

River as a basis for removing those links from any filed alternative route. 5 Applicants responded

VI.        ISSUES RAISED BY THE PARTIES: DUE PROCESS

           The ALJs summarized due-process concerns raised by numerous parties arising from the

compressed procedural schedule and notice deficiencies but declined to discuss whether the

schedule or procedures adopted to meet the 180-day deadline in PURA § 37.057 infringed upon

any party’s constitutional due-process rights. The PFD contends that the ALJs do not maintain

authority to resolve such constitutional questions, citing City of Dallas v. Stewart for the

proposition that an executive-branch agency such as SOAH lacks the power to resolve

constitutional challenges reserved exclusively to the judicial branch. 9


9

            The Brady Creek Intervenors except to the ALJs’ reliance on Stewart as a basis for

declining to weigh the due-process consequences of the ALJs’ own procedural rulings. Stewart is

not a SOAH case and has nothing to do with an administrative law judge’s ability to resolve

constitutional challenges in contested CCN cases. Stewart involved the Dallas Urban

Rehabilitation Standards Board, a thirty-member board of lay citizens with no legal training

requirement, which found Heather Stewart’s abandoned residence to be an urban nuisance and

ordered it demolished. The city of Dallas demolished the house while her appeal was still pending.

After the demolition, Stewart brought an inverse-condemnation claim under Article I, Section 17

of the Texas Constitution, and the question before the Texas Supreme Court was whether the

board’s nuisance finding could be given preclusive effect against that later, independently filed

takings claim in district court. 10 The Court held it could not, reasoning that mixed questions of law

and constitutionally relevant fact require de novo judicial review, and that substantial-evidence

review of a board’s finding did not adequately protect a takings claimant’s rights.

           Stewart addressed whether a lay citizen board’s nuisance determination, reviewable only

under a substantial-evidence standard, could be given preclusive effect against a landowner’s later,

independently filed takings claim under Article I, Section 17 of the Texas Constitution.11 The Texas

Supreme Court held that mixed questions of law and constitutionally relevant fact require de novo

judicial review, and that the board’s determination was accordingly not entitled to preclusive

effect. 12 The board in Stewart was not composed of attorneys, did not conduct any contested-case

comparable to the hearing conducted in this contested CCN proceeding.

           This proceeding, by contrast, was conducted before Administrative Law Judges in a

contested case with sworn testimony, an evidentiary record, and the extraordinarily limited right

to cross-examine adverse witnesses, now subject to Commission review of the ALJs’

recommendation through exceptions such as these. The question the Brady Creek Intervenors raise

is not whether SOAH may issue a binding constitutional ruling that forecloses later judicial review,

the concern Stewart addressed. The question is whether the ALJs’ own ruling denying the Brady

Creek Intervenors their own block of cross-examination time—and the numerous issues identified

in the PFD compounding on these due process concerns—left the ALJs without a complete record

on which to base the routing recommendation that follows and deprived the Brady Creek

Intervenors of their legal right to make said record.

           That question does not require resolving the constitutional questions within the holding of

Stewart; it requires only that the Commission consider whether the record underlying the PFD’s

routing recommendation comports with the requirements of due process. The ALJs’ own decision

to summarize the due process concerns below, “to give the Commission and any reviewing court

the fullest record,” 13 demonstrates that, throughout a contested CCN docket, the ALJs are very

much engaged in handling constitutional questions.

 VIII. ROUTING CRITERIA (Issues 8-10)

        The ALJs chose to spend 46 pages of the PFD (100-146) doing little other than reciting

their understanding of certain parties’ positions on certain issues or sub-issues on the routing

question. Many intervenor parties worked hard and invested significant resources to put on

thoughtful cases on which route should be selected.

        That effort was rewarded by the ALJs with less than two pages of a routing

recommendation that did little to resolve the issues set out in the preceding 46 pages. On routing,

the Commission is not faced with whether a different outcome would amount to the Commission

substituting its analysis for that performed by the ALJs. Rather, if the Commission reaches the

routing phase of the case, the task is to perform the first analysis of the evidence. A rigorous

analysis of the evidence, and application of the statutory and regulatory factors, leavened with a

little common sense, will invariably result in the selection of a route other than 894.

        If the Commission selects a route in this case, it should be Route 392 or Route 410.

        A. Overview of Proposed Routes

        The Brady Creek Intervenors except to the ALJ’s haphazard sampling of parties supporting

and opposing the various routes. The intervenor lists include factual inaccuracies and, without

basis in the record, lead the reader to assume that 894, which has twice as many supporters as

opponents listed, enjoys proportionally more support than, for instance, 392, which has twice as

many opponents listed as supporters. 20 Route selection is not a vote, and in this proceeding there

is no route that has obtained a majority of support among intervenors.
